intelligence.human_view: Imagine a master workshop with shelves of perfect parts — gauges, jewels, boards — each made once, made right, and the rule of the shop is that you never whittle a copy of a part when the real one is on the shelf. The shop is also a town you join, not a tool you sign up for: the town hands you a deed written in words you actually use, one piece at a time, and you are a citizen and a representative of the place, not a customer and not a salesperson. It is a theatre where the play is one story told the same way every night, but the manager does not judge the show by checking that the script printed correctly — she sits in a seat and watches it. And it is a shop that knows its regulars: members walk straight in to the main hall, visitors are shown the price board first, and when the shop gets paid, you get paid, with your account showing what's pending, what's official, what's paid.
intelligence.simple_view: In this workshop, all the pieces are already made, and they are beautiful. Your job is to pick the real piece off the shelf, not to draw a picture of it and pretend. Tap a day on the calendar and you see everything that happened that day. Being smart is doing the smartest thing: understand, pick wisely, do it right, and show that it worked. You can join free forever, and we never peek at your messages, ever. And we write everything so a brand-new person can understand it right away.
intelligence.grandma_view: Good houses run this way, dear. You keep a drawer of proper tools and you use them; you don't whittle a spoon every time you need to stir. A repair that only covers the crack will crack again — you fix the wall. And a cook doesn't serve a dish because the recipe was followed; she tastes it. Fair dealing is simple, dear: you pay your people when the money comes in, and you show them the book while they wait. The old inns had it right, love — the door is open to every traveller, and the paying rooms are listed plainly on the board. And you write a letter for the person reading it, dear, not for yourself — especially when they've never met you.
